title: Economic Evaluation of Community-Based Falls Prevention Interventions: A Methodological Survey of Evidence Synthesis Approaches

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Community-Based Falls Prevention and Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Burden of Falls in Community Settings
subsections.content:
Falls in community settings are a common and recurrent event among older adults, with incidence increasing sharply with age, frailty, multimorbidity, and prior fall history. Among community-dwelling populations, falls are not isolated accidents but a syndrome arising from the interaction of intrinsic risk factors—such as impaired balance, muscle weakness, cognitive impairment, visual deficits, and medication effects—with environmental hazards in the home and neighborhood. Epidemiologic work has shown that a substantial proportion of older adults fall each year, and many experience repeated falls, making falls prevention a core issue in healthy ageing and community care ref [1].

The burden of falls extends beyond immediate injury to include fractures, head trauma, fear of falling, activity restriction, loss of independence, institutionalization, and excess mortality. The consequences are also highly salient for health systems: fall-related emergency visits, hospital admissions, rehabilitation, long-term care use, and informal caregiving generate large downstream costs. Global burden analyses further indicate that falls are a leading cause of injury-related disability and death in later life, with substantial variation across countries but a consistently high contribution to years lived with disability among older adults ref [2].

For economic evaluation, this epidemiologic profile matters because the benefits of prevention are distributed across multiple sectors and time horizons. Community-based interventions may avert not only acute treatment costs but also deterioration in mobility, social participation, and quality of life, thereby justifying analytic frameworks that capture both health-service and broader societal consequences.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Community-Based Falls Prevention and Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Typology of Community-Based Falls Prevention Interventions
subsections.content:
Community-based falls prevention interventions can be classified by their principal mechanism of action and by whether they are delivered as single-component, multicomponent, or multifactorial strategies. A widely used typology distinguishes interventions targeting intrinsic risk factors—such as impaired balance, muscle weakness, visual deficits, medication-related risk, and fear of falling—from those targeting extrinsic hazards in the home or community environment. This distinction matters for economic evaluation because intervention complexity, required workforce, and expected pathways to benefit differ substantially across categories ref [3].

Exercise-based programmes constitute the most prominent intervention class in community settings and include balance and functional training, strength or resistance exercise, Tai Chi, gait training, and mixed regimens delivered individually or in groups. Other common categories are home safety assessment and modification, medication review or deprescribing support, vision-related interventions, and educational or behavioural programmes intended to improve adherence and risk awareness. Evidence syntheses suggest that exercise has the most consistent preventive effect among community-dwelling older adults, while the effects of other single-component interventions are often more context dependent ref [4].

A further distinction is between multicomponent interventions, in which the same package is offered to all participants, and multifactorial interventions, in which risk assessment is followed by individually tailored combinations of components. For reviewers of economic evidence, this typology is especially important because it shapes comparators, implementation costs, heterogeneity in outcomes, and the transferability of results across health and social care systems ref [3], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Community-Based Falls Prevention and Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Objectives and Scope of Economic Evaluation
subsections.content:
In community-based falls prevention, the core objective of economic evaluation is to inform whether interventions generate sufficient health gain, injury reduction, or downstream cost savings to justify use of limited public resources. This moves assessment beyond efficacy alone toward comparative value: which intervention, delivered to which population, and at what intensity, provides the greatest benefit for the resources required. Standard approaches include cost-effectiveness, cost-utility, and cost-benefit analysis, with the choice of framework depending on whether decision makers prioritize natural units such as falls prevented, preference-based outcomes such as quality-adjusted life years, or broader welfare impacts ref [6].

The scope of evaluation in this field is necessarily broad because falls prevention affects multiple sectors and time horizons. Relevant costs may include programme delivery, primary and hospital care, rehabilitation, long-term care, and informal care, while consequences may extend from avoided fractures and preserved functional independence to improved quality of life and reduced fear of falling. Methodological guidance therefore emphasizes explicit specification of analytic perspective, comparator, time horizon, discounting, and uncertainty, since these choices materially shape conclusions about value for money ref [7].

For community settings in particular, economic evaluation should also address heterogeneity and implementation conditions. The value of exercise, multifactorial assessment, home modification, or medication review may differ by baseline risk, adherence, and local service organization. Accordingly, the practical scope of evaluation includes both trial-based and model-based analyses, sensitivity analysis for key assumptions, and consideration of transferability across health and social care systems.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Community-Based Falls Prevention and Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Role of Systematic Reviews in Economic Evidence Synthesis
subsections.content:
Systematic reviews play a pivotal role in economic evidence synthesis for community-based falls prevention because the underlying literature is typically fragmented across intervention types, study designs, and decision contexts. By using explicit search, selection, and appraisal methods, reviews can identify whether apparent differences in cost-effectiveness reflect true variation in programme value or instead arise from heterogeneity in populations, comparators, time horizons, outcome measures, and analytic perspective. This is especially important in prevention, where modest short-term effects may translate into larger downstream benefits that are captured inconsistently across studies.

In practice, systematic reviews of economic evaluations do more than summarize incremental cost-effectiveness ratios. They assess methodological quality, transferability, and reporting completeness, helping readers judge whether evidence generated in one health system can inform decisions in another. Established guidance for reviewing economic evaluations emphasizes structured appraisal of resource-use measurement, valuation methods, modelling assumptions, and handling of uncertainty, thereby supporting more transparent cross-study comparison and interpretation ref [8].

For falls prevention specifically, evidence syntheses have shown that even when clinical reviews indicate benefit, the economic case may remain contingent on implementation format, participant risk profile, and local costs. Reviews focused on cost-effectiveness in older-person falls prevention have therefore been valuable in identifying both promising intervention classes and persistent evidence gaps, including limited comparability of outcomes and insufficient long-term modelling ref [9]. In this sense, systematic reviews provide the bridge between primary economic studies and policy-relevant conclusions about allocative efficiency.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations of Community-Based Falls Prevention and Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Definitional and Boundary Issues
subsections.content:
A central definitional issue is what counts as a “fall” and, relatedly, which outcomes should anchor evaluation. Trials and economic studies variably distinguish all falls, injurious falls, fractures, fall-related hospitalizations, and fear of falling, even though these outcomes capture different mechanisms of benefit and different cost consequences. The Prevention of Falls Network Europe recommended a standard definition of a fall and a core set of fall-related outcomes precisely to improve comparability across studies; without such harmonization, incremental cost-effectiveness estimates may reflect measurement choices as much as intervention performance ref [10].

Boundary-setting is equally important in defining “community-based” prevention. This category can include population screening in primary care, home hazard assessment, exercise delivered in senior centers, digitally supported balance training, or multifactorial programmes coordinated across health and social care. Such heterogeneity complicates decisions about the appropriate comparator, the relevant implementation costs, and whether spillovers beyond the health sector—such as informal care time, transport, or residential care avoidance—should be included. Recommendations from the Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine are useful here because they make explicit the choice between health care sector and societal perspectives and encourage transparent reporting of what is inside or outside the analytic boundary ref [11].

A further boundary issue concerns target population and time horizon. Falls prevention may be universal, risk-stratified, or disease-specific, and intervention value often depends on baseline frailty, prior falls, and adherence. Short trial horizons can miss downstream effects on disability, independence, and long-term care use, while overly broad modelling assumptions may overstate persistence of benefit. For this reason, surveys of the economic evidence must attend carefully to how studies define falls, delimit community settings, and justify perspective, comparator, and follow-up period.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Forms of Economic Evaluation
subsections.content:
Economic evaluations of falls prevention most commonly take the form of cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA), cost-utility analysis (CUA), and, less often, cost-benefit analysis (CBA). In this field, CEA typically reports incremental cost per fall prevented or per injurious fall avoided, whereas CUA expresses outcomes as cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained, facilitating comparison with interventions in other clinical areas. General methodological distinctions between these forms are well established in health economics and are especially relevant in falls prevention because interventions can generate both condition-specific outcomes and broader quality-of-life effects ref [6].

In practice, the choice of evaluative form strongly influences conclusions about value. Studies centered on short-term programme effects or trial end points often favor CEA using natural units such as number of falls averted. By contrast, evaluations intended to inform resource allocation across health sectors increasingly prefer CUA, since falls prevention may affect mobility, fear of falling, functional independence, and downstream care use beyond the immediate reduction in fall events. Reviews of the falls-prevention literature show substantial heterogeneity in outcome metrics, with many studies combining cost-consequence reporting alongside formal CEA or CUA, which complicates cross-study synthesis and threshold-based interpretation ref [9].

CBA remains uncommon in this area, partly because assigning monetary values to avoided falls, preserved independence, or reduced caregiver burden is methodologically and ethically contentious. Consequently, most contemporary studies frame falls prevention as a health sector investment assessed through CEA/CUA, while some broader public health analyses supplement these with disaggregated cost and outcome profiles rather than a single monetary net-benefit estimate ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Analytical Perspective and Costing Boundaries
subsections.content:
Analytical perspective is a decisive design choice in economic evaluations of falls prevention because it determines which consequences are counted as relevant costs and benefits. In this field, many studies adopt a health care payer or health system perspective, emphasizing intervention delivery costs, emergency presentations, hospital admissions, rehabilitation, and residential care triggered by fall-related injury. However, guidance from the Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine argues that a broader societal perspective should also be considered, particularly when interventions affect unpaid caregiving, patient time, transport, and downstream social care use that may be substantial in older populations ref [11].

Costing boundaries are therefore especially important for multifactorial and community-based falls interventions, whose resource implications often extend beyond the medical sector. Restricting analysis to acute health service costs can understate value when programmes reduce informal care needs, delay functional decline, or prevent transitions into long-term care, whereas including these components can materially improve estimated cost-effectiveness. By contrast, broader costing may also capture participant time and programme coordination costs that make apparently low-cost interventions less favorable. Methodological reviews of falls-prevention economics repeatedly note heterogeneity in perspective and cost inclusion as a major reason why estimates are difficult to compare across studies and jurisdictions ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Time Horizons and Discounting Practices
subsections.content:
Time horizon is a consequential design choice in economic evaluations of falls prevention because intervention effects may emerge gradually and extend beyond the follow-up period observed in trials. Short horizons, often limited to 6–12 months, can capture immediate reductions in falls or fall-related service use but may understate downstream consequences such as fracture avoidance, delayed institutionalization, or sustained quality-of-life gains. Methodological guidance therefore recommends that the analytic horizon be long enough to reflect all important differences in costs and outcomes between alternatives, rather than merely mirroring study duration ref [6].

In the falls prevention literature, this creates a recurring tension between trial-based evaluations, which commonly adopt short observation windows, and model-based analyses, which extrapolate over multiple years or the remaining lifetime to reflect recurrent fall risk and age-related morbidity. Longer horizons may be especially relevant where interventions alter functional trajectory or reduce serious injurious falls, but they also require stronger assumptions about persistence of effect, adherence decay, and mortality. Reviews of economic evaluations in falls prevention have consequently noted substantial heterogeneity in chosen horizons, which complicates cross-study comparison and transferability of cost-effectiveness results ref [9].

Discounting practices follow the same logic: when costs and health outcomes accrue beyond one year, both should usually be discounted at the rate recommended by the jurisdictional guideline being applied. In practice, discount rates vary across studies because evaluations align with national reference cases, and some short-term trial analyses omit discounting altogether. For falls prevention, these choices can materially affect incremental results, particularly when interventions incur upfront implementation costs but generate benefits only over longer periods.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Comparators and Usual Care Definitions
subsections.content:
Comparator choice is a major source of heterogeneity in economic evaluations of falls prevention. Studies variously compare an intervention with no active program, waiting-list control, attention control, or “usual care,” yet these alternatives are rarely equivalent in practice. In falls prevention, usual care can already include medication review, opportunistic advice, referral to physiotherapy, or community exercise options, so incremental cost-effectiveness depends heavily on how comprehensively the baseline package is specified. This issue is especially salient because multifactorial assessment and management are often judged against care pathways that differ across health systems and even across trial sites ref [4].

Poorly defined comparators can bias both within-study and cross-study interpretation. A program may appear highly cost-effective when contrasted with minimal service provision, but much less so when evaluated against an established falls clinic, exercise referral scheme, or broader geriatric care package. The clinical falls literature has long emphasized that intervention effects are contingent on the background level of prevention activity and on whether controls receive co-interventions that reduce fall risk ref [3]. For economic evaluation, this implies that authors should describe usual care as a resource bundle rather than a label, and should justify whether the relevant policy comparator is current practice, best available practice, or an incremental add-on to existing services.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Trial-Based Versus Model-Based Evaluations
subsections.content:
Falls prevention studies use both trial-based and model-based economic evaluations, and the choice materially affects the scope of inference. Trial-based evaluations are grounded in observed resource use and outcomes collected alongside randomized or pragmatic studies, giving them strong internal validity and close correspondence to the intervention as delivered. However, in falls prevention they are often constrained by short follow-up, limited statistical power for rare but costly events such as hip fracture or long-term care admission, and difficulty capturing downstream quality-of-life gains beyond the trial period, as highlighted in reviews of the field ref [9].

Model-based evaluations address these limitations by extrapolating beyond observed data and synthesizing evidence across multiple sources. Decision trees or Markov models can represent recurrent falls, fracture pathways, mortality, institutionalization, and sustained intervention effects over longer horizons, making them particularly useful when prevention benefits accrue gradually or differ across risk strata. Yet these advantages come at the cost of stronger structural assumptions regarding transition probabilities, persistence of effect, adherence, and baseline risk; accordingly, the credibility of model-based results depends heavily on transparent model specification, validation, and extensive sensitivity analysis ref [13].

In practice, the two approaches are complementary rather than competing. Trial-based analyses are most informative for estimating short-run, context-specific cost-effectiveness, whereas model-based studies are better suited to lifetime or policy-level questions, transferability across settings, and comparisons among multiple intervention options not tested head-to-head. For falls prevention, where consequences may unfold over years and span health and social care sectors, hybrid strategies that use trial data to populate or validate decision models are often methodologically preferable ref [9], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Designs and Analytical Frameworks in Economic Evaluation
subsections.subsection_title: Handling Uncertainty and Sensitivity Analysis
subsections.content:
Handling uncertainty is particularly consequential in economic evaluations of falls prevention because estimates are often driven by relatively infrequent but high-cost events, heterogeneous baseline risk, imperfect adherence, and uncertain longer-term maintenance of intervention effects. Good practice therefore requires uncertainty analysis to move beyond simple one-way variation and to distinguish parameter, methodological, and structural uncertainty. In applied work, this means testing assumptions about fall rates, fracture probabilities, intervention uptake, persistence of benefit, and health-state utilities, all of which can materially alter incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.

Probabilistic sensitivity analysis is especially important when model outputs depend on multiple correlated inputs, and it is now widely recommended as the reference approach for representing joint parameter uncertainty in decision models ref [15]. Results are most informative when reported as cost-effectiveness planes and acceptability curves, rather than as point estimates alone. For trial-based evaluations, uncertainty should also reflect sampling variation, missing data, and skewed cost distributions; non-parametric bootstrap methods have been recommended to characterize the joint distribution of incremental costs and effects in such settings ref [16].

In the falls prevention literature, however, sensitivity analysis has often been narrower than these standards, with deterministic scenario analyses used more frequently than formal exploration of structural assumptions. This matters because choices about recurrent-fall modelling, risk stratification, and extrapolation beyond trial follow-up may be at least as influential as uncertainty in individual parameters. Transparent justification of scenario choices, alongside probabilistic analysis where feasible, is therefore essential for interpreting whether apparent cost-effectiveness is robust or contingent on modeling assumptions.

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Falls-Related Outcome Metrics
subsections.content:
Falls prevention economic studies use a heterogeneous set of effectiveness endpoints, ranging from number of falls, proportion of participants experiencing at least one fall, and recurrent fallers, to injurious falls, fractures, hospitalisations, and fall-related deaths. These metrics are not interchangeable: rate-based outcomes capture repeated events and are often more sensitive to intervention effects, whereas dichotomous outcomes such as “at least one fall” may understate benefits in populations with frequent recurrent falls. The choice of endpoint therefore directly affects both estimated effectiveness and the translation of effects into costs and utilities ref [4].

A further challenge is the inconsistent definition and ascertainment of a fall-related event. Consensus work has emphasized standardised definitions of a fall and recommended common domains for reporting, including falls, recurrent falls, injuries, fractures, healthcare use, and psychological consequences such as fear of falling ref [17]. In practice, studies differ in whether outcomes are self-reported or prospectively recorded in calendars, whether injuries are medically verified, and whether minor and major injuries are combined, generating substantial between-study variation in measured event rates.

For economic evaluation, this variability matters because different outcome metrics map onto resource consequences with different precision. Preventing a non-injurious fall may have limited short-run cost implications, while preventing an injurious fall or fracture can avert substantial downstream expenditure. Reviews of falls prevention trials have also shown that intervention effects are often stronger for rate of falls than for fractures or institutional outcomes, so analysts must be explicit about which falls-related metric anchors the economic case and how surrogate endpoints are linked to broader health and cost consequences ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Preference-Based Health Outcomes and QALYs
subsections.content:
Preference-based health outcomes are central to economic evaluation because they permit effects of falls prevention to be expressed as quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), facilitating comparison with interventions in other clinical areas. In practice, however, QALY gains in falls studies are often modest and difficult to detect over short follow-up periods. Generic preference-based instruments may be insensitive to changes that matter in this field, such as fear of falling, confidence in mobility, or maintenance of independence, particularly when interventions primarily avert infrequent but severe events rather than produce immediate average health-status gains ref [18].

A further challenge is the choice and valuation of the utility instrument. Reviews of quality-of-life measurement in older populations have highlighted heterogeneity in the use of EQ-5D, SF-6D, Health Utilities Index, and mapping approaches, each with different descriptive systems and value sets, making cross-study comparison difficult ref [19]. For falls prevention, these differences are consequential because mobility, pain, self-care, and usual activities domains can respond differently depending on baseline frailty and injury severity. Utility decrements from fractures or hospitalization may be substantial but transient, whereas benefits from preserving confidence and functional autonomy may be diffuse and undercaptured.

Accordingly, interpretation of QALY-based results in this literature requires attention to timing, instrument sensitivity, and whether utilities were measured directly or extrapolated from external sources. Where QALYs appear small despite reductions in falls or injurious falls, this may reflect measurement limitations as much as limited intervention value.

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Direct, Indirect, and Informal Care Costs
subsections.content:
Cost identification in falls prevention studies varies substantially by analytic perspective. Narrow health-care perspectives typically include hospitalisation, emergency department use, outpatient care, rehabilitation, medications, and residential aged-care costs attributable to falls, whereas broader societal perspectives additionally capture patient time, transport, productivity losses, and unpaid care. This distinction matters because falls often trigger extended recovery pathways rather than isolated acute episodes, so evaluations limited to immediate treatment costs may underestimate the economic consequences of both injurious and non-injurious falls ref [1].

Indirect costs are especially heterogeneous in older populations. Lost paid productivity is often modest after retirement, but opportunity costs still arise through disrupted unpaid work, volunteer activity, and caregiver time. Informal care can be a major post-fall cost component when mobility declines, fear of falling increases supervision needs, or a fall precipitates transition from independent living to supported care. Methodological guidance from the Second Panel supports transparent reporting of such non-health-care consequences alongside the valuation approach used for time and unpaid care, yet many evaluations either omit these costs or include them inconsistently, limiting comparability across studies ref [11].

A further challenge is separating costs caused by the index fall from those associated with multimorbidity and frailty. Resource use following a fall may reflect intertwined trajectories of disability, recurrent falls, and institutionalisation, making attribution sensitive to follow-up duration and data source. Reviews of falls-prevention economics have therefore noted wide variation in whether studies include downstream long-term care and informal support, with important implications for estimated cost savings and conclusions about value for money ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Resource Use Measurement and Costing Methods
subsections.content:
Resource use measurement in falls prevention studies is highly heterogeneous, with variation in both the items counted and the instruments used to capture them. Evaluations may include intervention delivery inputs such as staff time, training, equipment, transport, venue hire, and participant time, but many studies differ in whether they also measure downstream health and social care use after a fall. Trial-based analyses often rely on self-report diaries or recall for hospital visits, primary care contacts, and community services, whereas administrative datasets can improve completeness for acute care but may miss social care, home support, and privately purchased services. This inconsistency reduces comparability across studies and contributes to differences in estimated cost-effectiveness even for similar interventions ref [9].

Costing methods add a second layer of variation. Some studies use micro-costing to value intervention components in detail, while others apply gross-costing or average reimbursement schedules; the choice can materially affect estimates for multifactorial and exercise-based programs delivered across settings. Standard economic evaluation texts emphasize the need to distinguish quantities of resources from unit prices, report the price year, and state whether costs reflect opportunity cost, tariffs, or charges ref [6]. For falls prevention, this is especially important because unit costs for emergency care, rehabilitation, residential care, and community support differ substantially across jurisdictions.

A further challenge is the treatment of implementation and scale-up costs. Reviews of falls prevention economics note that recruitment, adherence support, and ongoing program maintenance are often undermeasured, despite their importance for real-world affordability and transferability ref [12]. Greater transparency in resource inventories, data sources, and valuation assumptions is therefore essential for interpreting and comparing economic evidence.

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Equity-Relevant and Non-Health Outcomes
subsections.content:
Falls prevention can generate important benefits that are only partially reflected in conventional health-care payer analyses. Distributional issues are especially salient because fall risk, injury severity, and access to effective interventions vary by age, frailty, socioeconomic position, housing conditions, and rurality. The Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine explicitly recommends a broader impact inventory so that consequences falling outside the health sector are identified and, where relevant, valued alongside health outcomes ref [11]. In falls prevention, this includes consequences for social care use, caregiver time, residential transitions, and the ability of older adults to remain safely independent at home.

Non-health outcomes are also central to intervention benefit. Fear of falling, confidence in mobility, social participation, and functional independence may improve even when changes in QALYs are modest, particularly because generic preference-based instruments can be insensitive to domains such as balance confidence or activity avoidance. Reviews of falls interventions in primary care show that reducing fear of falling is itself a meaningful patient-relevant outcome, with implications for activity, isolation, and subsequent service use ref [18]. Excluding such effects risks undervaluing multifactorial or exercise-based programmes whose main gains are maintenance of autonomy and participation rather than large short-term mortality effects.

For equity-relevant appraisal, studies should therefore report subgroup effects where possible and make transparent whether benefits accruing to carers or the social care sector were omitted. Emerging guidance on falls prevention for older adults also emphasizes person-centred outcomes and heterogeneity in risk, reinforcing the need for evaluations that move beyond narrowly defined injury counts or health-service costs alone ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Outcome Measurement, Cost Components, and Valuation Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Attribution and Valuation of Long-Term Benefits
subsections.content:
Attributing long-term benefit in falls prevention is methodologically difficult because short-trial reductions in falls must often be translated into downstream changes in fractures, hospitalisation, residential care entry, mortality, and quality-adjusted survival. This requires assumptions about the persistence of intervention effects, recurrence risk, and the causal pathway from a fall event to later disability or dependency. In practice, many economic evaluations rely on decision-analytic extrapolation beyond observed follow-up, making structural assumptions about maintenance or waning of effect particularly influential on cost-effectiveness estimates ref [13], ref [14].

Valuation is further complicated by the fact that benefits may accrue across multiple sectors and over long periods. Avoided hip fractures and head injuries can generate future savings in acute care, rehabilitation, and long-term care, while preserving mobility and independence may also delay institutionalisation and reduce informal caregiving needs. Capturing these benefits requires time horizons long enough to reflect downstream consequences and explicit handling of competing mortality risks in older populations; otherwise, studies may systematically undervalue preventive interventions whose major gains occur after the trial period ref [13], ref [6].

Accordingly, credible falls-prevention evaluations should make transparent the assumptions linking intermediate outcomes to longer-term endpoints, justify the duration of treatment effect, and test alternative extrapolation scenarios. Sensitivity analysis around durability of benefit, fracture risk reduction, and residential care transitions is especially important because these parameters often drive incremental cost-effectiveness results more strongly than short-run programme costs alone ref [14], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Search Strategies and Inclusion Criteria
subsections.content:
In reviews of economic evidence on community-based falls prevention, search strategy design is a major determinant of completeness because relevant studies are often dispersed across clinical, public health, rehabilitation, and health economics journals. Methodological guidance for systematic reviews of economic evaluations recommends combining biomedical databases with specialist economic sources and using broad terminology for both the intervention and the economic component, rather than relying only on cost-effectiveness indexing terms, which are inconsistently applied ref [8]. In this field, narrow searches can miss trial-based cost analyses embedded within effectiveness studies or model-based evaluations published outside dedicated economics outlets.

Eligibility criteria also shape review yield and interpretability. Reviews commonly differ in whether they include only full economic evaluations, or also partial evaluations such as cost analyses and cost descriptions; whether they restrict to community-dwelling older adults; and how they define multicomponent or setting-bridging interventions. For falls prevention specifically, intervention taxonomies developed in major effectiveness reviews provide a useful basis for structuring inclusion criteria around exercise, home hazard modification, medication review, vision-related strategies, and multifactorial programmes ref [4]. However, inconsistent application of these categories at review level can lead to heterogeneous evidence pools and complicate comparison across reviews.

A recurring limitation is inadequate reporting of date limits, language restrictions, hand-searching, and procedures for identifying companion economic papers linked to effectiveness trials. Transparent specification of population, intervention, comparator, perspective, study design, and minimum outcome requirements is therefore essential, particularly where reviews aim to synthesize both cost-effectiveness and broader resource-use evidence ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Quality Assessment Tools for Economic Studies
subsections.content:
A recurring methodological issue in reviews of economic evidence on community-based falls prevention is the inconsistent use of appraisal instruments tailored to economic evaluation. Reviews often apply generic risk-of-bias tools designed for effectiveness studies, yet these do not adequately address key economic domains such as costing methods, valuation of outcomes, time horizon, discounting, uncertainty analysis, and the appropriateness of modelling assumptions. For trial- and model-based studies alike, the Drummond checklist remains one of the most widely recognized frameworks because it explicitly examines whether alternatives, costs, consequences, and analytic methods are clearly and appropriately specified ref [6].

Where reviews include model-based evaluations, stronger appraisal is achieved when reporting and structural validity are considered alongside basic checklist compliance. The Philips framework is particularly relevant in this context because it extends quality assessment beyond transparency of inputs to the justification of model structure, data identification, consistency checks, and handling of uncertainty ref [20]. In falls prevention, this matters because cost-effectiveness estimates are sensitive to assumptions about recurrent falls, downstream injury pathways, adherence, and longer-term care use.

Accordingly, higher-quality systematic reviews should distinguish between reporting quality and methodological quality, and should match the appraisal tool to study design rather than applying a single undifferentiated instrument across all included studies. Doing so improves interpretability of review findings and helps identify whether apparent differences in cost-effectiveness arise from intervention effects or from weaknesses in the underlying economic methods.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Methods for Data Extraction and Evidence Synthesis
subsections.content:
In reviews of economic evidence on community-based falls prevention, data extraction must usually extend beyond basic study descriptors to include analytic perspective, time horizon, price year, discounting, resource-use categories, outcome metric, modelling approach, and characterization of uncertainty. Because primary studies often report costs and effects inconsistently, reviewers commonly need structured extraction templates that separate trial-based from model-based evaluations and record whether incremental estimates are directly observed or modelled. Guidance on systematic reviews of economic evaluations emphasizes that extraction should also capture transferability factors, including setting, unit costs, and assumptions about intervention implementation, since these strongly condition cross-study comparability ref [21].

Evidence synthesis is rarely amenable to conventional quantitative pooling. Economic evaluations differ in currencies, costing methods, outcome measures, and willingness-to-pay thresholds; in falls prevention, heterogeneity is compounded by variation in intervention intensity, participant risk profile, and follow-up duration. As a result, narrative and tabular synthesis remains the dominant approach, often supplemented by cost standardization to a common price year and currency and by grouping studies according to intervention type or analytic framework. Methodological critiques of economic review practice note that attempts to aggregate incremental cost-effectiveness ratios can be misleading, and recommend instead comparing the direction and robustness of conclusions, the sources of uncertainty, and the structural assumptions underlying models ref [8].

Where synthesis spans both trial-based and modelled studies, a useful strategy is to present results in layered form: first the original study findings, then any reviewer-led standardization, and finally an interpretive synthesis of drivers of cost-effectiveness. For falls prevention reviews, this is particularly important because conclusions may hinge less on point estimates than on assumptions about adherence, recurrent falls, injury severity, and health-related quality-of-life decrements.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Assessment of Review-Level Bias and Transparency
subsections.content:
Assessment of review-level bias in syntheses of economic evidence for community-based falls prevention should extend beyond appraisal of included studies to the review process itself. Key risks include selective inclusion of cost studies, inconsistent handling of multiple publications from the same evaluation, inadequate documentation of currency conversion or price-year standardization, and post hoc restriction of perspectives, outcomes, or jurisdictions. Such choices can materially alter conclusions about apparent cost-effectiveness even when the underlying primary studies are unchanged. Review teams therefore need explicit protocols and transparent decision rules for study selection, data hierarchy, and treatment of overlapping evidence, consistent with broader guidance on assessing bias in systematic reviews [1].

Transparency is equally important because economic reviews often involve interpretive judgments that are less standardized than effect-size meta-analysis. Use of protocol registration, disclosure of deviations from planned methods, full search strategies, reproducible extraction templates, and clear reporting of funding sources and conflicts of interest improves credibility and allows readers to distinguish between evidential limitations and review-induced uncertainty. PRISMA 2020 reinforces these expectations by emphasizing protocol accessibility, comprehensive reporting of methods, and explanation of synthesis decisions; these elements are especially pertinent where heterogeneity precludes quantitative pooling and narrative synthesis dominates [2].

In practice, many reviews of falls-prevention economics remain only partially transparent: they summarize conclusions on cost-effectiveness but provide limited information on excluded records, duplicate screening, or how review authors reconciled discordant model assumptions across settings. A structured review-level bias appraisal, coupled with reproducible reporting, is therefore essential before policy conclusions from review evidence are used to prioritize community implementation.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Treatment of Heterogeneity Across Reviews
subsections.content:
Heterogeneity is a central challenge in reviews of economic evidence on community-based falls prevention because variation arises simultaneously in intervention content, target risk profile, comparator choice, analytic perspective, time horizon, outcome metric, and national price year. In practice, this means that studies evaluating exercise, multifactorial assessment, home modification, or medication review are often too dissimilar for direct quantitative pooling, even when they address a common policy question. Guidance on incorporating economic evaluations in systematic reviews therefore emphasizes structured tabulation and transparent categorization of design features before any cross-study comparison is attempted ref [21].

Across reviews, heterogeneity is most appropriately handled through narrative or framework-based synthesis rather than meta-analysis of incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, which are not statistically or conceptually straightforward to combine. Review authors commonly group evidence by intervention type, setting, country, and economic evaluation method, and then interpret results in light of transferability and decision context. This approach is particularly important in falls prevention, where intervention effectiveness and resource use depend on local service delivery arrangements and baseline fall risk, limiting the external validity of pooled economic conclusions ref [12].

A recurring limitation, however, is that many reviews describe heterogeneity but do not explicitly distinguish between clinical, methodological, and jurisdictional sources of variation, nor do they consistently explore how these differences drive divergent cost-effectiveness findings. More rigorous treatment would involve prespecified subgrouping, standardized currency and price-year conversion where feasible, and explicit discussion of why synthesis stops at qualitative comparison rather than unsupported quantitative aggregation ref [21], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Appraisal of Systematic Reviews of Economic Evidence
subsections.subsection_title: Reporting Standards and Reproducibility
subsections.content:
Reporting of reviews of economic evidence in community-based falls prevention should enable readers to reconstruct how cost and outcome data were identified, selected, transformed, and compared. In practice, reproducibility is often weakened when reviews provide only high-level summaries of intervention categories or cost-effectiveness conclusions, without transparent reporting of price years, currency conversions, inflation adjustments, analytic perspective, or the decision rules used to judge transferability across settings. Broader reporting guidance for systematic reviews is therefore directly relevant, particularly the expectation that searches, selection processes, data items, synthesis methods, and availability of extracted data be described in sufficient detail to permit replication ref [23].

For the economic component specifically, reproducibility also depends on how clearly review authors document the extraction and interpretation of resource-use categories, valuation methods, time horizons, discounting, and uncertainty analyses from included studies. CHEERS was developed for primary economic evaluations rather than systematic reviews, but its domains provide a useful benchmark for what review authors should report when summarizing economic methods and assumptions across studies ref [7]. In this topic area, stronger practice would include publishing study-level extraction tables, reporting all standardization steps for monetary outcomes, distinguishing author-reported from reviewer-derived estimates, and making protocols, analytic code, and supplementary files publicly accessible. Such measures improve auditability and help users judge whether apparent differences in cost-effectiveness reflect true intervention effects or merely inconsistent reporting and reviewer interpretation.

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Variation by Country and Health System Context
subsections.content:
Variation by country and health system context is a central reason why economic conclusions from systematic reviews cannot be read as universally applicable. Even when intervention effects are similar, estimates of cost-effectiveness can shift substantially across settings because unit costs, service utilization patterns, baseline fall risk, workforce availability, and funding arrangements differ between tax-funded systems, social insurance models, and mixed public–private systems. Cross-national comparative work in health systems has long shown that institutional design shapes both resource use and prices, implying that the same falls-prevention programme may generate different incremental costs and downstream savings in different jurisdictions [1].

For community-based falls prevention, contextual heterogeneity is especially important because interventions often depend on local delivery infrastructure, such as primary care referral pathways, rehabilitation services, and social care coordination. International guidance has emphasized that recommended falls strategies must be adapted to local epidemiology, workforce capacity, and implementation constraints rather than assumed to transfer unchanged across countries [2]. As a result, reviewers should interpret pooled economic findings with caution, paying attention to the country of origin, perspective, and health-system architecture of included studies.

From a policy perspective, variation across contexts does not make evidence unusable; rather, it changes the level at which conclusions should be drawn. Reviews are often more informative about the likely direction of value, the main cost drivers, and the conditions under which interventions become attractive than about a single transferable ICER. This reinforces the need for local adaptation, including re-parameterization with country-specific costs, service pathways, and target population risk profiles before results are used to support reimbursement or public health decisions.

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Transferability of Cost-Effectiveness Evidence
subsections.content:
Transferability of cost-effectiveness evidence is a central concern when applying review findings across jurisdictions. Even when intervention effects are clinically similar, incremental cost-effectiveness ratios may shift substantially because of differences in unit costs, baseline fall risk, service delivery pathways, uptake, adherence, and the valuation of health outcomes. As a result, economic conclusions from one country cannot be assumed to hold elsewhere without explicit assessment of contextual fit and parameter uncertainty ref [25].

Frameworks for transferability distinguish between aspects that may be relatively portable (for example, core intervention mechanisms) and those that are highly context dependent, such as resource use, prices, epidemiology, and comparators in usual care ref [26]. For falls prevention in older adults, this means that programmes relying on allied health capacity, home modification markets, or primary care referral systems may appear efficient in one setting but not in another. Review authors should therefore emphasize disaggregated reporting of costs, resource quantities, and subgroup effects so that decision makers can recalibrate models using local data rather than import headline ratios.

In practice, the most policy-relevant synthesis is not a simple ranking of published ICERs, but an assessment of which model structures, assumptions, and inputs are transferable to the target setting. This favors adaptable decision models and scenario analyses over direct numerical adoption of foreign estimates, particularly where health system organization or social care financing differs materially.

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Implementation, Scalability, and Real-World Feasibility
subsections.content:
Economic findings from trials or tightly controlled programmes often overstate value when implementation conditions are weaker in routine care. For falls prevention, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness depend not only on intervention efficacy but also on uptake, adherence, provider skill mix, coordination across health and social care, and sustained delivery fidelity. Pragmatic implementation considerations are therefore central to interpretation: interventions shown to be efficient in research settings may lose value when participation is low, when exercise intensity is diluted, or when referral pathways fail to reach those at greatest risk.

Frameworks from implementation science help explain these gaps. RE-AIM emphasises reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance as distinct determinants of population impact, highlighting why scalable interventions may differ from those that perform best in efficacy studies ref [27]. Similarly, the MRC guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions argues that context, mechanisms, and implementation quality should be examined alongside outcomes, which is especially relevant for multicomponent falls programmes delivered across community, primary care, and social support settings ref [28].

For policy, this implies that review-level economic conclusions should be read with attention to workforce capacity, training requirements, monitoring costs, and the feasibility of long-term maintenance. Decision makers may place greater weight on interventions with slightly less favourable incremental ratios if they are simpler to embed, easier to scale, and more robust under real-world constraints. Recent falls guidelines likewise stress integration, tailoring, and system readiness, reinforcing that scalable value is a function of delivery infrastructure as much as of intervention design ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Targeting High-Risk Populations and Stratified Value
subsections.content:
Targeting high-risk populations is a recurrent strategy for improving the value proposition of prevention programmes, because absolute benefit, and therefore expected cost offsets, often rises with baseline risk. In falls prevention, this implies that interventions may appear only marginally cost-effective when offered universally, yet become more attractive when directed to older adults with prior falls, balance impairment, frailty, medication-related risk, or multimorbidity. This logic is consistent with broader work on heterogeneity in cost-effectiveness, which argues that average incremental cost-effectiveness ratios can conceal substantial subgroup variation relevant to policy design ref [29].

For cross-context interpretation, stratified value depends not only on clinical effect modification but also on local case-mix, service delivery costs, uptake, and the distribution of risk factors across communities. Reviews of falls prevention have repeatedly noted that multifactorial and exercise-based interventions tend to generate greater benefit in groups at elevated risk, although the operational definition of 'high risk' varies across studies and health systems ref [4]. As a result, transferability is strongest when decision makers can map trial subgroups onto locally identifiable populations and when routine data support risk stratification in practice.

However, targeted delivery also raises equity and implementation questions. Restricting eligibility can improve efficiency while missing socially vulnerable individuals whose risk is under-recorded or whose access to assessment is limited. A policy-relevant interpretation of stratified value therefore requires attention to both distributional consequences and the feasibility of identifying, engaging, and retaining high-risk groups under real-world conditions ref [29], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Decision Thresholds and Willingness-to-Pay
subsections.content:
Interpretation of cost-effectiveness evidence is inseparable from the decision threshold applied in the target jurisdiction. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios that appear favorable in one setting may not represent good value elsewhere because thresholds embody local opportunity costs, budget constraints, and social preferences rather than universal constants. This is especially important for community and prevention interventions, where benefits may accrue over long horizons and outside the health sector, making threshold choice materially influential on conclusions about adoption or disinvestment ref [6].

A further complication is that willingness-to-pay thresholds are often treated as fixed benchmarks despite substantial debate about their empirical basis. Claxton and colleagues argued that thresholds should reflect the health forgone when resources are displaced within constrained systems, implying that historically used thresholds may be too high in some settings ref [31]. By contrast, in public health and social care, decision makers may also give weight to broader capability, independence, caregiver effects, and equity concerns, so a single health-sector QALY threshold may understate perceived social value.

For systematic reviews, this means pooled economic conclusions should be interpreted cautiously unless results are expressed in ways that can be re-mapped to local thresholds, currencies, and perspectives. Reporting net monetary benefit across a range of threshold values, rather than relying only on point ICERs, improves policy relevance and makes explicit how judgments change under alternative willingness-to-pay assumptions ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Cross-Context Comparability, Transferability, and Policy Relevance
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Public Health and Social Care Policy
subsections.content:
For public health and social care policy, the central implication of the economic review literature is that falls prevention should not be treated solely as a narrow clinical service question. Because benefits often accrue across sectors—health care, social care, informal care, and longer-term independence—policy interpretation depends on whether decision makers adopt a health-sector or broader societal perspective. The Second Panel’s recommendations reinforce the importance of making these perspective choices explicit, particularly where interventions may shift costs between medical services and community support systems rather than simply reduce total expenditure ref [11].

Policy relevance also depends on whether evidence is translated into delivery models that reflect local implementation constraints. Frameworks developed for real-world public health emphasize that reach, adoption, implementation fidelity, and maintenance are integral to population impact; these dimensions are especially pertinent for community falls programmes that require coordination across primary care, rehabilitation, housing, and voluntary-sector providers ref [27]. As a result, interventions that appear efficient in trial-based analyses may generate limited policy value if workforce capacity, referral pathways, or sustained participation are weak.

A further implication is that policy appraisal should consider not only average cost-effectiveness but also who benefits. Distributional approaches highlight that interventions can improve aggregate health while also affecting equity across socioeconomic or clinical risk groups ref [30]. For social care policy, this supports targeting strategies that prioritize older adults at highest risk of injury, recurrent falls, or functional decline, while remaining attentive to access barriers that could otherwise widen inequalities.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Understudied Interventions and Populations
subsections.content:
A persistent evidence gap in economic evaluations of community-based falls prevention is the narrow range of interventions and populations studied. Most analyses have focused on relatively healthy, community-dwelling older adults receiving exercise, home hazard modification, or multifactorial programs, while far less is known about approaches tailored to people with cognitive impairment, severe frailty, sensory loss, or multimorbidity. This matters because intervention effectiveness, adherence, resource use, and downstream consequences are likely to differ substantially across these groups, and reviews of falls prevention have repeatedly noted limited subgroup-specific evidence despite marked heterogeneity in risk profiles and care pathways ref [4].

Understudied intervention types also deserve greater economic attention. Psychological and behavioral components, including interventions targeting fear of falling, may influence activity restriction, social participation, and subsequent health service use, yet they remain underrepresented in cost-effectiveness work relative to exercise-centered models. Evidence syntheses suggest that fear of falling is an important and modifiable outcome in primary care and community settings, but translation of these effects into preference-based outcomes and long-term economic consequences is still limited ref [18]. Future studies should therefore prioritize inclusive recruitment, pre-specified heterogeneity analyses, and designs capable of evaluating hybrid or tailored packages for high-risk subgroups, including ethnically diverse, socioeconomically disadvantaged, and rural populations.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Integration of Equity and Distributional Economic Evaluation
subsections.content:
Equity remains weakly integrated in economic evaluations of community-based falls prevention, despite clear social patterning in both falls risk and access to preventive services. Most studies estimate average cost-effectiveness for a notional older population, which can obscure whether benefits accrue disproportionately to healthier, wealthier, or more service-connected groups. A more informative approach is to combine subgroup-specific estimates of baseline risk, intervention uptake, adherence, and outcomes with explicit social value judgements about inequality, as formalized in distributional cost-effectiveness analysis ref [30].

For falls prevention, this implies moving beyond conventional subgroup analysis toward models that quantify trade-offs between total health gain and its distribution across deprivation, ethnicity, rurality, frailty, disability, or housing insecurity. Practical applications could link intervention reach and effectiveness to socially stratified risks of recurrent falls, injury, and care use, then evaluate whether targeted delivery narrows or widens health inequalities. Extended frameworks such as equity-informative cost-effectiveness analysis are also relevant where interventions generate important non-health consequences, including unpaid caregiver burden, out-of-pocket costs, or differential capability to age safely at home ref [32].

Future methodological work should therefore pre-specify equity-relevant strata, justify the choice of inequality metrics and social welfare functions, and report distributional assumptions transparently. This would help align falls prevention evaluation with broader public health goals, especially where community programmes are intended not only to reduce injuries efficiently, but also to improve fairness in later-life independence and access to preventive care.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Use of Real-World Data and Linked Administrative Sources
subsections.content:
Real-world data and linked administrative sources offer an important route for strengthening the economic evidence base for community-based falls prevention, particularly where trial follow-up is short and relatively uncommon but costly outcomes such as fracture, hospital admission, residential care entry, and mortality are poorly captured. Routine data can improve estimation of downstream service use and costs, support external validation of model assumptions, and enable assessment of intervention reach and persistence under usual-care conditions rather than tightly controlled trial settings. The value of linkage is especially clear when moving from intermediate outcomes, such as reduced fall rates, to health-system consequences that matter for economic evaluation.

Methodologically, however, administrative datasets are not neutral substitutes for trial data. Falls are incompletely recorded in many routine systems, coding practices vary across settings, and linked datasets may better identify injurious falls than recurrent non-injurious events, creating potential bias in both effectiveness and cost estimates. These issues are compounded by confounding, selective uptake of community programmes, and informative missingness in social care and functional status variables. Guidance on real-world evidence for decision making emphasizes the need for explicit design choices, transparent analytic protocols, and careful consideration of data provenance and fitness for purpose ref [33], ref [34].

For future work, linked hospital, primary care, ambulance, mortality, and aged-care records could be used to parameterize recurrent-event models, quantify spillovers across sectors, and estimate subgroup-specific pathways for older adults with multimorbidity or prior falls. A useful agenda is therefore not only greater use of routine data, but stronger reporting standards for linkage quality, outcome definitions, and bias mitigation, so that real-world evidence can be credibly incorporated into model-based and trial-based economic evaluations of falls prevention ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Advanced Modeling of Recurrent Falls and Complex Pathways
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation in economic evaluations of community-based falls prevention is the use of simple cohort models that treat falls as a one-off event or collapse recurrent episodes into an average annual probability. This is poorly aligned with the clinical reality that falls are recurrent, history-dependent, and clustered within high-risk periods after an initial event. Future models should therefore move beyond standard Markov structures toward recurrent-event, semi-Markov, or individual-level state-transition approaches that can represent event dependence, time since last fall, competing mortality, and changing frailty over time, consistent with broader good-practice recommendations for decision modelling in health economics ref [13].

More advanced structures are also needed to capture complex causal pathways linking intervention uptake, adherence, functional status, fear of falling, injury severity, hospital admission, long-term care transition, and quality-of-life loss. In this context, multistate methods offer a principled framework for representing transitions among non-injurious falls, injurious falls, disability, institutionalization, and death, while allowing intervention effects to operate on several pathways rather than only on fall incidence ref [36]. Such models would be especially valuable for synthesizing heterogeneous evidence from multifactorial interventions, where benefits may arise through mobility, confidence, or activity changes as much as through direct reduction in falls.

Methodological priorities include explicit handling of heterogeneity and treatment-effect modification, joint modelling of repeated falls and downstream costs, and validation against external epidemiologic and service-use data. Greater use of patient-level simulation may also improve estimation of accumulated risk and equity-relevant subgroup effects, but this will require better reporting of transition assumptions, recurrence parameters, and structural uncertainty than is typical in current studies ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Standardization of Methods in Review and Primary Evaluation
subsections.content:
A persistent barrier to cumulative learning in the economic literature on community-based falls prevention is the lack of standardization across both primary evaluations and evidence syntheses. Studies continue to differ in analytic perspective, time horizon, outcome selection, handling of recurrent falls, and valuation of intervention delivery and downstream care, limiting comparability and transferability. Greater uptake of established reporting standards for economic evaluation and systematic review reporting would improve transparency and make cross-study synthesis more defensible, particularly where decision makers need to compare multicomponent interventions implemented in heterogeneous community settings [1,2].

Standardization is also needed in outcome definition and measurement. In falls prevention, consensus work has already demonstrated the feasibility of harmonizing core domains such as falls, injurious falls, and related consequences for trials [3]. Extending this logic to economic evaluation would support more consistent linkage between effectiveness endpoints, resource use, and quality-of-life impacts, while encouraging routine reporting of implementation characteristics, adherence, intervention intensity, and uncertainty analyses in forms that can be reused in meta-analysis or model-based synthesis.

For future reviews, a more explicit methodological minimum dataset would be valuable: extraction of price year, costing approach, perspective, unit-cost sources, utility instrument, model structure, and treatment of recurrent events. For primary studies, alignment around these elements would not eliminate contextual variation, but it would substantially reduce avoidable heterogeneity and strengthen the evidentiary base for comparative and distribution-sensitive assessment.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Gaps, Emerging Methods, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Agenda for Future Systematic Methodological Overviews
subsections.content:
Future systematic methodological overviews in community-based falls prevention should move beyond cataloguing intervention results and instead map how economic evidence is produced, synthesized, and judged. A priority is to develop review frameworks that classify studies by decision problem, analytic perspective, handling of recurrent falls, treatment of intervention implementation, and approach to heterogeneity and uncertainty. This would help address long-recognized weaknesses in reviews of economic evaluations, including inconsistent appraisal criteria and limited ability to explain why results differ across settings and methods ref [8].

A second priority is to make methodological overviews explicitly comparative across review designs. Reviews should examine how authors identify economic studies, integrate model-based and trial-based evaluations, assess transferability, and manage overlapping evidence bases. Existing guidance on including economic evaluations in systematic reviews provides a foundation, but a more focused programme of overviews is needed for falls prevention to identify where generic review methods fail to capture sectoral complexity, such as cross-sector costs, multifactorial pathways, and repeated-event outcomes ref [21].

Finally, future overviews should adopt a meta-research orientation: prospectively registered protocols, explicit risk-of-bias assessment for reviews themselves, and structured comparison of reporting quality, decision-analytic assumptions, and data sources over time. Such work could generate a methodological roadmap for the field, support greater consistency in evidence synthesis, and clarify when pooled economic conclusions are appropriate versus when narrative, context-sensitive synthesis is more defensible.
